skala_force_chop_compound_do_expression #

Arrangement of binary expressions — Force chop compound condition in 'do' statement. Implemented in BreakPlan.PlanForcedChopCondition. ⚠ The earlier note here — that the oracle chops 'whether the operators are all &&, all || or mixed' — is refuted: re-measured one key at a time, a mixed condition is chopped at the root operator's own kind only, so do { } while (a.P && b.P || c.P) breaks at the || and stays whole at the &&. A two-operand chain is chopped only when neither operand is a single token, which is why while (a && b) never moves at either value. Governs the do statement alone.

skala_force_chop_compound_if_expression #

Arrangement of binary expressions — Force chop compound condition in 'if' statement. Implemented in BreakPlan.PlanForcedChopCondition. ⚠ The earlier note here — that the oracle chops 'whether the operators are all &&, all || or mixed' — is refuted: re-measured one key at a time on conditions that all fit, the chop takes the root operator's own kind only, so if (a.P && b.P || c.P) breaks at the || and stays whole at the &&. Three clauses, all measured: only &&/|| roots (a relational, a single &, and an is combinator do not move); three or more operands always chop; a two-operand chain chops only when neither operand is a single token, so if (a && b), if (a && b.P) and if (a > 0 && b) stay on one line while if (a.P && b.P) and if (F() && G()) chop. Not a width rule — a > 0 && b and F() && G() are the same ten columns and go opposite ways. Governs the if statement alone, else if included.

skala_force_chop_compound_while_expression #

Arrangement of binary expressions — Force chop compound condition in 'while' statement. Implemented in BreakPlan.PlanForcedChopCondition. ⚠ The earlier note here — that the oracle chops 'whether the operators are all &&, all || or mixed' — is refuted: re-measured one key at a time, a mixed condition is chopped at the root operator's own kind only, so while (a.P && b.P || c.P) breaks at the || and stays whole at the &&. A two-operand chain is chopped only when neither operand is a single token, which is why while (a && b) never moves at either value. Governs the while statement alone; the do statement's trailing condition has its own key.
